title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: The number in the name is the mass number A. Find Z (the protons) on the periodic table, then neutrons = A − Z.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Ask what each unit describes: a curie measures how radioactive the source is (activity); a sievert measures the dose a person receives.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Divide by the becquerels in one curie to get curies, then convert curies to microcuries (1 Ci = 10<sup>6</sup> μCi). Keep the sig figs of the given activity.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Compare each isotope with the stable P-31. Which decay turns a neutron into a proton, and which turns a proton into a neutron? Then find the new Z on the periodic table.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: An alpha particle is <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He. Subtract 4 from the top number and 2 from the bottom number, then look up the new element by its Z.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: A beta particle is <sup>0</sup><sub>−1</sub>e. The top number stays the same; what must the daughter's bottom number be so the bottom numbers add up?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: A positron is <sup>0</sup><sub>+1</sub>e. Keep the top number; the daughter's Z plus 1 must equal oxygen's Z. Look up that element.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Add the top numbers and the bottom numbers on the left, then subtract what is already on the right. Which particle has the leftover A and Z?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Think about penetrating power: alpha is stopped by paper, beta by a few millimeters of light material, and gamma needs something dense.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{6}\)
hint: The proton is <sup>1</sup><sub>1</sub>H and the alpha particle is <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He. Total the left side, subtract the alpha particle, and look up the element with the leftover Z.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{7}\)
hint: Two neutrons add 2 to the top and nothing to the bottom. Total the left side, subtract the alpha particle (4 on top, 2 on bottom), and identify the element.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{8}\)
hint: Protons = Z and neutrons = A − Z for each nucleus. If A stays the same and a proton turned into a neutron, which decay does that?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Find the number of half-lives first: time ÷ half-life. Then halve the activity once for each half-life (an arrow map works well).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Draw an arrow map from the starting mass, halving each time until you reach 4.00 mg. Count the arrows, then multiply by the half-life.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Divide the time by the half-life to get the number of half-lives (a whole number), then multiply the mass by (1/2) that many times.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: Count half-lives (time ÷ half-life), then start an arrow map at 100% and halve once per half-life.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Write the half-life as an equality, 1 half-life = 13 h, and use it as a conversion factor on 39 h. Then halve 8.00 mCi once per half-life.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{6}\)
hint: Make a percent arrow map from the whole sample, halving until you reach 12.5%. Count the arrows and multiply by the half-life.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: What fraction of carbon-14 is left after exactly one half-life? Compare that with the charcoal's percent.
why: One half-life leaves 50% of the original carbon-14, and the half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Build a percent arrow map from the full amount down to 6.25%. Count the arrows, multiply by 5730 years, and report three significant figures.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Carbon-14 dating works only on things that were once alive, and only up to about 50,000 years. Check each object against both conditions.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\) (Challenge)
hint: Challenge item: use the top-and-bottom rule. The left side totals 1 + 235 on top; remember the 3 in front of the neutrons counts 3 on top. Then find the element from Z.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: What do control rods absorb? Fewer of those particles means fewer new fissions.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Fusion joins two nuclei; what charge do nuclei carry, and what happens when like charges are pushed together? What charge does the neutron that starts fission have?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: Use the inverse-square law: dose rate is proportional to 1/d<sup>2</sup>. By what factor does d<sup>2</sup> change when the distance goes from 1.0 m to 2.0 m, and to 3.0 m?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: Alpha particles cannot get through skin or a container. Radon is a gas: where does it end up once it is breathed in?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Which cells divide rapidly? Think about what happens when DNA is damaged and copied before repair enzymes can fix it.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
hint: For imaging, the radiation must leave the body to reach the camera, and the activity should fade quickly. Compare the radiation types and half-lives of the two isotopes.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
hint: What does the thyroid use iodine for? Can the body tell a radioactive iodine atom from a stable one?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
hint: Ask whether the radiation is made by a machine outside the patient or by decaying nuclei inside the patient. Which of these can be turned off?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
hint: (a) A positron is <sup>0</sup><sub>+1</sub>e; Z drops by 1. (b) Count half-lives: time ÷ half-life. (c) How much would be left after a few hours of shipping?

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
hint: Check the green sheet solubility rules for nitrates. What would a dissolved Ba<sup>2+</sup> ion do in the body, compared with insoluble BaSO<sub>4</sub>?

title: Problem 14.1
hint: Radioactivity comes from the atoms themselves. Which choices describe other discoveries: X-rays, the Curies' new elements, or radioactivity made by bombardment?

title: Problem 14.2
hint: The number in each name is A. Find Z on the periodic table; neutrons = A − Z. The "m" does not change either count.

title: Problem 14.3
hint: Sort the four units: which measure the activity of a source, which measures energy absorbed per kilogram, and which adjusts for biological effect?

title: Problem 14.4
hint: (a) Go mCi → Ci → Bq → MBq with conversion factors (1 Ci = 3.7 × 10<sup>10</sup> Bq). (b) First find how many MBq equal 1 mCi.

title: Problem 14.5
hint: (a) 1 mSv = 100 mrem. (b) Divide by the limit and multiply by 100%. (c) Divide by the dose of one X-ray. (d) Compare with 3 mSv.

title: Problem 14.6
hint: (a) Bq → Ci → μCi with 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10<sup>10</sup> Bq. (b) 1 pCi = 0.037 Bq. (c) Divide the body's activity by one banana's. Keep two significant figures.

title: Problem 14.7
hint: An image needs to show where the gamma rays came from, live. Which detector records the position of each gamma ray as it strikes?

title: Problem 14.8
hint: Use the top-and-bottom rule: subtract the alpha particle's 4 from the top and 2 from the bottom. Then check each choice's top and bottom numbers.

title: Problem 14.9
hint: In beta decay the top number stays the same and Z goes up by 1. Find each parent's Z, add 1, and look up the new element.

title: Problem 14.10
hint: A positron has 0 on top and +1 on the bottom. Which choice keeps A the same and makes the bottom numbers add up?

title: Problem 14.11
hint: (a) In electron capture, write <sup>0</sup><sub>−1</sub>e on the left, as a reactant. (b) Compare what happens to A and Z in each, and which side the electron or positron appears on.

title: Problem 14.12
hint: For each, subtract the right side from the left: top numbers give the missing A, bottom numbers give the missing Z. Match A and Z to a particle.

title: Problem 14.13
hint: Work backward: add the top numbers and the bottom numbers on the right side. The parent has those totals; look up the element by its Z.

title: Problem 14.14
hint: Total the top and bottom numbers on the left, then subtract what is already on the right. A gamma ray (0 on top, 0 on bottom) adds nothing.

title: Problem 14.15
hint: Compare the top and bottom numbers on both sides of the equation. What does the m in 99m mean, and what does the gamma ray carry away?

title: Problem 14.16
hint: Ionizing power and penetrating power run in opposite directions. Which radiation is heaviest and most highly charged?

title: Problem 14.17
hint: (a) Find which shield first drops each reading to the background of 30 cpm. (b) Which reading is still above background behind lead? (d) Think about radiation released inside the body.

title: Problem 14.18
hint: Rank alpha, beta, and gamma by penetrating power. What could stop an alpha particle before it reaches someone below the ceiling?

title: Problem 14.19
hint: Count half-lives (time ÷ half-life), then halve 48.0 ng that many times. Each half-life halves what is left, not the original.

title: Problem 14.20
hint: Find the number of half-lives: time ÷ half-life. Then halve 12.0 mCi once per half-life with an arrow map.

title: Problem 14.21
hint: (a) One-fourth is (1/2) multiplied by itself how many times? Multiply that number by the half-life. (b) Take that fraction of the starting activity.

title: Problem 14.22
hint: (a) Halve once for each 6-hour step. (b) Count the hours from 7:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m. the next day, divide by 6.0 h, and halve that many times.

title: Problem 14.23
hint: (a) How long does the activity take to fall to half? (b) Count half-lives in 90.0 h and halve from 96.0. (c) Keep halving from the last row of the table.

title: Problem 14.24
hint: Make an arrow map from 64.0 μg down to 2.00 μg and count the halvings. Then divide the time by that count.

title: Problem 14.25
hint: Count half-lives: 39 h ÷ 13 h. Going back in time the activity must get bigger, so double once per half-life instead of halving.

title: Problem 14.26
hint: Does the half-life of an isotope depend on how much you have, or on temperature and storage? Apply the definition of half-life to each vial.

title: Problem 14.27
hint: Keep halving: 50%, 25%, 12.5%, and so on. Count how many halvings it takes to go below 1%.

title: Problem 14.28
hint: (a) Multiply the number of half-lives by 13 h, then convert hours to days. (b) Ten half-lives means dividing by 2<sup>10</sup>; then convert mCi to μCi.

title: Problem 14.29
hint: Carbon-14 dating needs something that was once alive and an age under about 50,000 years. Check each choice against both.

title: Problem 14.30
hint: Compare 5300 years with the half-life of carbon-14, 5730 years. How much carbon-14 is left after exactly one half-life, and has that much time passed yet?

title: Problem 14.31
hint: (a) What keeps adding fresh carbon-14 to a living tree? (b) What changes once it is cut? (c) Carbon-14 is a beta emitter; use the top-and-bottom rule.

title: Problem 14.32
hint: Make an arrow map from the living-plant count rate, halving until you reach the mat's rate. Count the arrows, multiply by 5730 years, and keep three significant figures.

title: Problem 14.33
hint: Write 1/64 as (1/2)<sup>n</sup> to find the number of half-lives. Then check each choice for both the value and the significant figures (5730 has three).

title: Problem 14.34
hint: (a) Divide the age by 5730 years and round to a whole number. (b) Multiply 100% by (1/2) that many times. (c) How many counts would so little carbon-14 give?

title: Problem 14.35
hint: Make a percent arrow map from the rain value down to 12.5% and count the arrows. Multiply by tritium's half-life.

title: Problem 14.36
hint: (a) In electron capture the electron goes on the left; Z drops by 1. (b) Make a percent arrow map from the full amount to 25.0%, count the arrows, and multiply by the half-life.

title: Problem 14.37
hint: Is the Sun's energy from a chemical or a nuclear change? Which nuclear process joins light nuclei and which splits heavy ones, and what is the Sun mostly made of?

title: Problem 14.38 (Challenge)
hint: Challenge item: the bottom numbers already balance. Total the top numbers on each side; the difference is the number of neutrons.

title: Problem 14.39 (Challenge)
hint: Challenge item: total the left side (include the neutron that starts fission). Subtract the iodine and all three neutrons from the top, and the iodine's Z from the bottom.

title: Problem 14.40 (Challenge)
hint: Challenge item: total the top and bottom numbers on the left, then subtract what is on the right. In (b), the missing amount is shared by two identical particles.

title: Problem 14.41
hint: Fewer free neutrons means fewer new fissions. Which part of the reactor controls how many neutrons are free, and which way should it move?

title: Problem 14.42
hint: Fission is a nuclear change, not burning. Compare the total mass of the products with the reactants: which way does it change when energy is released?

title: Problem 14.43
hint: (a) 8.50% means Diablo Canyon's output is 0.0850 of the total; divide to find the total. (b) What heats the water in a nuclear plant? (c) See the spent-fuel discussion in 14.5.

title: Problem 14.44
hint: Radiation damages DNA most in cells that divide often. Which tissue makes new blood cells all the time?

title: Problem 14.45
hint: (a) Inverse-square law: dose rate is proportional to 1/d<sup>2</sup>; how does d<sup>2</sup> change when the distance doubles? (b) Dose = dose rate × time; convert minutes to hours. (c) How many half-lives is 8.0 days?

title: Problem 14.46
hint: (a) 1 pCi = 0.037 decays per second; then multiply by 3600 s/h. (c) Alpha: subtract 4 on top, 2 on bottom. (e) Count half-lives: 7.6 days ÷ 3.8 days.

title: Problem 14.47
hint: (a) How many times farther is 1.5 m than 0.50 m? Use the inverse-square law. (b) Dose = dose rate × time in hours. (c) Time, distance, and what else?

title: Problem 14.48
hint: X-rays and gamma rays are both electromagnetic radiation. Where is each made, and which one stops when the power is turned off?

title: Problem 14.49
hint: Gamma rays are the most penetrating and least ionizing. Can they change a nucleus in the product they pass through?

title: Problem 14.50
hint: Treatment needs radiation that stays in the target organ; imaging needs gamma rays that leave the body and a short half-life. Which pairing fits both?

title: Problem 14.51
hint: (a) Alpha: subtract 4 on top and 2 on bottom. (b) Divide 34.2 days by the half-life, then halve 6.60 MBq that many times. (c) How far do alpha particles travel?

title: Problem 14.52
hint: Imaging with a gamma camera needs gamma rays and a short half-life; PET needs a positron emitter. (d) Use an arrow map from 20.0 mCi down to 5.00 mCi.

title: Problem 14.53
hint: (a) Divide the sample ratio by the living ratio, then write it as (1/2)<sup>n</sup>. (b) Multiply n by 5730 years. (c) Compare with about 50,000 years. (d) Cosmic-ray neutrons hit nitrogen-14.

title: Problem 14.54
hint: (a) Use the top-and-bottom rule. (c) Count half-lives in 220 min; going back in time, double once per half-life. (d) Halve from 100% until below 1%, then convert to hours.

title: Problem 14.55
hint: (a) Only alpha decays change A, by 4 each; find how many, then use beta decays to fix Z. (c) Count half-lives in 15.2 days and halve 3.20 ng.

title: Problem 14.56
hint: Compare iodine-131's neutron count with the stable iodine-127. Which decay turns a neutron into a proton?

title: Problem 14.57
hint: For each choice, ask what part of the atom changes in a chemical reaction and in a nuclear reaction. Can heating or a catalyst change a nucleus?

title: Problem 14.58
hint: Bombardment: the particle that strikes goes on the left. Total the top and bottom numbers on each side, and remember a coefficient multiplies both numbers of a particle.

title: Problem 14.59
hint: Protons = Z and neutrons = A − Z for both nuclei. A did not change; did a proton become a neutron or the reverse?

title: Problem 14.60
hint: (a) Write 1 half-life = 30.2 years as a conversion factor. (b) Arrow map from 100%, one arrow per half-life. (c) Multiply 1.20 g by that fraction.

title: Problem 14.61
hint: (a) A positron is <sup>0</sup><sub>+1</sub>e, so Z drops by 1. (b) Count half-lives in 38.1 h and halve 4.00 mCi. (c) Which radiation can leave the body to reach a detector?

title: Problem 14.62
hint: Alpha particles are stopped by dead skin outside the body. Radium is in Group 2 like calcium; where does it settle once swallowed?

title: Problem 14.63
hint: Contrast agents block X-rays; is the barium in BaSO<sub>4</sub> radioactive? Use the green sheet: is BaSO<sub>4</sub> soluble?
